glossary.d: (yellow pages) and read about the sickness in the book.
The part of the body that contains the stomach, liver, and guts. The belly.
Different from what is usual, natural, or average. Not normal.
A sac of pus caused by bacterial or other infection. For example, a boil.
(pimples) A skin problem causing bumps on the face, chest, or back that form small white 'heads' of pus or sometimes 'blackheads' of dirt. Most common in young people (adolescents).
Sudden and short-lived. An acute illness is one that starts suddenly and lasts a short time. The opposite of 'chronic'.
An emergency condition of the abdomen that often requires a surgical operation. Severe pain in the belly with vomiting and no diarrhea may mean an acute abdomen.
The years in which a child becomes an adult. The teens: 13 to 19 years old. Afterbirth See Placenta.
A continual need a person cannot control to overuse alcoholic drinks such as beer, rum, wine, etc.
A problem such as an itching rash, hives, sneezing, and sometimes difficult breathing or shock that affects certain people when specific things are breathed in, eaten, injected, or touched.
(also amoebas) Tiny animals that live in water or in the gut and can only be seen with a microscope. They can cause diarrhea, dysentery, and liver abscess.
Loss of a body part.
Medicine to calm pain.
A disease in which the blood gets thin for lack of red blood cells. Signs include tiredness, pale skin, and lack of energy. See also Pernicious anemia.
Medicine used to control too much stomach acid and to calm stomach upset.
Medicine that fights infections caused by bacteria.
Vomit-control medicine. A medicine that helps keep people from vomiting or feeling nauseated.
Medicine used to treat allergies such as hay fever and itching. Also helps control vomiting and causes sleepiness.
A soap or cleaning liquid that prevents growth of bacteria.
Medicine used to relieve cramps or spasms of the gut.
Medicine that acts against or neutralizes a poison or toxin. Often made from the blood serum of horses.
(anti-venin) An antitoxin used to treat poisoning from a venom, such as snake poison.
The opening at the end of the gut between the legs; asshole.
The main artery or vessel that carries blood out of the heart to the body.
An old word for stroke. See Stroke.
A finger-like sac attached to the large intestine (gut).
Something that is easiest, safest, and most likely to work in a particular situation or condition. 420
A vessel carrying blood from the heart through the body. Arteries have a pulse. Veins, which return blood to the heart, have no pulse.
(roundworm) Large worms that live in people's intestines and cause discomfort, indigestion, weakness, and sometimes gut obstruction (blocking of the gut).
Tiny germs that can only be seen with a microscope and that cause many different infectious diseases.
The sac inside the womb that holds the baby; amniotic sac. When it breaks, releasing its fluid, this usually means that labor has begun.
Chronic open sores that appear in people who are so ill they do not roll over or change position in bed.
The act of casting a spell or influencing by witchcraft; hexing. Some people believe that they get sick because a witch has bewitched them or given them the 'evil eye'
A bitter, green liquid made by the liver and stored in the gallbladder. It helps digest fat. Birth defects See Defects.
A small plug or 'head' of dirt blocking a pore in the skin of the face, chest, or back. A kind of pimple. Bladder stones See kidney stones.
The force or pressure of the blood upon the walls of the blood vessels (arteries and veins); it varies with the age and health of the person.
A swollen, inflamed lump with a pocket of pus under the skin. A kind of abscess.
A repeat vaccination to renew the effect of an earlier series of vaccinations.
To have a bowel movement is to defecate; to shit; the way of passing solid waste out of the body.
Trade name. The name a company gives to its product. A brand–name medicine is sold under a special name and is often more expensive than the same generic medicine. Breast abscess See Mastitis.
A birth in which the baby comes out buttocks or legs first.
A medicine that works against many kinds of micro-organisms. Compare with a narrow-spectrum antibiotic, which works against only a few.
The tubes leading to the lungs, through which air passes when a person breathes.
An infection of the bronchi.
A very swollen lymph node. Bubos is a common name for lymphogranuloma venereum.
The part of the body a person sits on; ass, arse, rump, behind, backside, butt.
A tumor or lump that grows and may keep growing until it finally causes death.
Starches and sugars. Foods that provide energy.
(manioc, yucca) A starchy root grown in the tropics.
A stiff bandage of gauze and plaster that holds a broken bone in place until it heals.
An eye problem in which the lens of the eye becomes cloudy, making it more and more difficult for the person to see. The pupil looks gray or white when you shine a light into it.
A rubber tube used to drain urine from the bladder.
A hole or spot of decay in a tooth where bacteria have got in and destroyed part of the tooth.
(C.) A measure or scale of heat and cold. A healthy person's temperature (normal temperature) is 37° C. Water freezes at 0° C. and boils at 100° C. Cerebro-vascular accident, CVA See Stroke.
The opening or neck of the womb at the back of the vagina.
A painless sore or ulcer on the genitals, finger, or lip that is one of the first signs of syphilis.
A tiny, crawling spider or tick like animal that buries its head under the skin and sucks blood.
Health Chart A monthly record of a child's weight that shows whether the child is gaining weight normally. 421
(This is also called childbed fever, womb infection, postpartum infection, or puerperal infection.) The fever and infection that mothers sometimes develop after childbirth.
Long-term or frequently recurring (compare with acute). A chronic disease is one that lasts a long time.
The flow of blood through the arteries and veins by the pumping of the heart.
Divided, separated. A child born with a cleft palate has a separation or abnormal opening in the roof of his mouth. Climacteric Menopause.
Sharp abdominal pains caused by spasms or cramps in the gut.
The first milk a mother's breasts produce. It looks watery but is rich in protein and helps protect the baby against infection.
A state of unconsciousness from which a person cannot be wakened. It is caused by disease, injury, or poison, and often ends in death.
A group of people living in the same village or area who have similar living conditions, interests, and problems.
Secondary health problems that sometimes develop in the course of a disease. For example, meningitis may result as a dangerous complication of measles.
A mixture of plant and animal waste that is allowed to rot for use as a fertilizer. Hay, dead leaves, vegetable waste, animal droppings, and manure all make good compost.
A folded cloth or pad put on a part of the body. It may be soaked in hot or cold water.
A thin, protective layer that covers the white of the eye and inner side of the eyelids.
See Loss of consciousness.
Dry, hard, difficult stools (bowel movements) that do not come often.
An old name for tuberculosis.
Touch. Contagious diseases can be spread by a sick person coming in contact with (touching or being close to) another person.
A sickness that can be spread easily from one person to another
To dirty, stain, or infect by contact. A syringe that has not been boiled is often contaminated and can cause infections, even though it looks clean.
Any method of preventing pregnancy.
Tightening or shortening of muscles. The strong contractions of the womb when a woman is in labor help to push the baby out of the womb.
Shortened or tight muscles in a joint that limit movement.
A situation or condition when a particular medicine should not be taken. (Many medicines are contraindicated in pregnancy.)
An uncontrolled fit. A sudden jerking of part or all of the person's body, as in meningitis or epilepsy.
The clear outer layer or 'window' of the eye, covering the iris and pupil.
Hard, thick, painful parts of the skin formed where sandals or shoes push against the skin or one toe presses against another.
A painful tightening or contraction of a muscle.
See Hypothyroidism.
A home remedy that consists of drawing blood to the surface of the body by use of a glass or cup with a flame under it.
An abnormal, sac-like, liquid-filled growth developing in the body.
Oily white or grayish flakes or scales that appear in the hair. Seborrhea of the scalp.
A medicine that helps relieve swelling or stuffiness of the nose or sinuses.
Birth defects are physical or mental problems a child is born with, such as a hare lip, club foot, or an extra finger or toe.
Not having enough of something; a lack.
Abnormally formed, not having the right shape.
A condition in which the body loses more liquid than it takes in. This lack of water is especially dangerous in babies.
A state of mental confusion with strange movements and speech; it may come with high fever or severe illness. *Dermal Of the skin.
An infection or irritation of the skin. 422
Reddish, irritated patches between a baby's legs caused by urine in his diapers (nappy) or bedding.
Frequent runny or liquid stools.
The kinds and amounts of foods that a person should eat or avoid eating.
A release or flowing out of fluid, mucus, or pus.
Bones that have slipped out of place at a joint
A way to wash out the vagina by squirting a stream of water up into it.
When a person stops breathing (suffocates) from being under water.
Diarrhea with mucus and blood. It is usually caused by an infection.
Sudden seizures, especially during pregnancy or childbirth, very dangerous for both mother and baby.
The beginnings of an unborn baby when it is still very small.
A sudden sickness or injury that calls for immediate attention.
A medicine or drink that makes people vomit. Used when poisons have been swallowed.
A solution of water put up the anus to cause a bowel movement.
An outbreak of disease affecting many persons in a community or region at the same time.
A study to find out the worth or value of something, or how much has been accomplished. Often done by comparing different factors or conditions before and after a project or activity is underway.
A glance or look from someone believed to have the power to bewitch or do harm to people.
Extreme fatigue and tiredness.
A medicine that helps a person cough up mucus from the respiratory tract (lungs, bronchi, etc.); a cough-helper.
The month and year marked on a medicine that tells when it will no longer be good. Throw away most medicines after this date.
(F.) A measure or scale of heat and cold. A healthy person's temperature (normal temperature) is 98.6° F. Water freezes at 32° F. and boils at 212° F.
Using birth control methods to plan when to have and not have children.
Being able to see things at a distance better than things close at hand.

Stools; shit; the waste from the body that is moved out through the bowels in a 'bowel movement'. Feces–to–mouth Spread or transmitted from the stools of one person to his or another person's mouth, usually by food or drink, or on fingers.
An instrument or tool for listening to sounds made by the unborn baby (fetus) inside the womb.
(foetus) The developing baby inside the womb.
A body temperature higher than normal.
Emergency care or treatment for someone who is sick or injured.
A bad cold, often with fever, pain in the joints, and sometimes diarrhea.
Worms that infect the liver or other parts of the body and cause different diseases. Blood flukes get into the blood and cause schistosomiasis. Foetus See Fetus.
A nutritious substance found in leafy green vegetables. Follicles Small lumps.
The 'soft spot' on the top of a young baby's head. Fracture A broken bone.
A great or sudden fear.
A small, muscular sac attached to the liver. The gallbladder collects bile, a liquid that helps digest fatty foods.
Soft, loosely woven kind of cloth used for bandages.
The scientific name of a medicine, as distinct from the brand names given it by different compainies that make it. 423
The organs of the reproductive system, especially the sex organs.
Very small organisms that can grow in the body and cause some infectious diseases; microorganisms.
A microscopic parasite that can infect the intestines, causing frothy yellow diarrhea.
A simple form of sugar that the body can use quickly and easily. It is found in fruits and honey, and can be bought as a white powder for use in Rehydration Drinks.
A swelling on the lower front of the neck (enlargement of the thyroid gland) caused by lack of iodine in the diet.
(gr.) A unit of weight based on the weight of a grain of wheat. 1 grain weighs 65 mg.
(gm.) A metric unit of weight. There are about 28 grams in an ounce. There are 1000 gm. in 1 kilogram.

The front part of the body where the legs join. The genital area. Gut Intestines. Gut thread or gut suture material A special thread for sewing or stitching certain wounds, and especially tears from childbirth. The gut thread is slowly absorbed (disappears) so that the stitches do not need to be taken out.
A split in the upper lip, going from the mouth up to the nose (like a hare, or rabbit). Some babies are born with a hare lip.
A person who takes part in making his community a healthier place to live.
A burning feeling in the lower chest or upper part of the stomach.
Severe or dangerous bleeding.
(piles) Small, painful bumps or lumps at the edge of the anus or inside it. These are actually swollen or varicose veins.
A plant, especially one valued for its medicinal or healing qualities.
Passed on from parent to child.
(rupture) An opening or tear in the muscles covering the belly that allows a loop of the gut to push through and form a ball or lump under the skin.
A magic spell or jinx said to be caused by a witch.

(medical history) What you can learn through asking questions about a person's sickness—how it began, when it gets better or worse, what seems to help, whether others in the family or village have it, etc.
Hard, thick, raised spots on the skin that itch severely. They may come and go all at once or move from one place to another. A form of allergic reaction.
Chemicals made in parts of the body to do a special job. For example, estrogen and progesterone are hormones that regulate a woman's period and chance of pregnancy.
Actions or practices of personal cleanliness that lead to good health.
High blood pressure.
Very rapid, deep breathing in a person who is frightened.
Extreme worry or concern over an imagined sickness.
A condition in which a child is born mentally slow and often deaf. It is usually due to lack of iodine in the mother's diet.
(1) In common language, a condition of great nervousness, fear, and emotional distress. (2) In medical terms, signs of sickness caused by fear or the power of belief.
(vaccinations) Medicines that give protection against specific diseases, for example: diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, polio, tuberculosis, and measles.
A sickness caused by bacteria or other germs. Infections may affect part of the body only (such as an infected finger) or all of it (such as measles).
A disease that is easily spread or communicated (passed from one person to another); contagious.
An area that is red, hot, and painful, often because of infection.
A poison that kills insects. DDT and lindane are insecticides.
A condition in which a person is not able to sleep, even though he wants and needs to.
A substance (enzyme) produced by the pancreas, which controls the amount of sugar in the blood. Injections of insulin are sometimes needed by persons with diabetes.
Worms and tiny animals that get in people's intestines and cause diseases. 424
The guts or tube-like part of the food canal that carries food and finally waste from the stomach to the anus.
(IM) injection An injection put into a muscle, usually of the arm or the buttock—different from an intravenous (IV) injection, put directly into a vein.
The slipping of one portion of the gut into one nearby, usually causing a dangerous obstruction or blocking of the gut.
The colored or dark part of the eye around the pupil.
A yellow color of the eyes and skin. It is a sign of disease in the liver, gallbladder, pancreas, or blood.
A dullness and softening of the eye, ending in blindness. It is caused by a lack of vitamin A.
Large, bean-shaped organs in the lower back that filter waste from the blood, forming urine.

Small stones that form in the kidneys and pass down to the urinary tube. They can cause a sharp pain in the lower back, side, urinary tube, or lower belly. In the bladder they may block the urinary tube and make urination painful or impossible.
(kg.) One thousand grams. A 'kilo' is equal to a little over 2 pounds.
(wet malnutrition) Severe malnutrition. A child with kwashiorkor has swollen feet, hands, and face, and peeling sores.
The sudden tightening or contractions of the womb that mean the baby will soon be born.
(larvae) The young worm-like form that comes from the egg of many insects or parasites. It changes form when it becomes and adult.
An outhouse; privy; a hole or pit in the ground to use as a toilet.
A medicine used for constipation that makes stools softer and more frequent.
Tough cords in a person's joints that help hold them in place.
Of or relating to the tongue.
(l.) A metric measure equal to about one quart. A liter of water weighs one kilogram.
A large organ under the lower right ribs that helps clean the blood and get rid of poisons.
The condition of a sick or injured person who seems to be asleep and cannot be wakened. Unconsciousness.
An oil or cream used to make surfaces slippery.

Small lumps under the skin in different parts of the body that are traps for germs. They become painful and swollen when they get infected. In tuberculosis and cancer they are often swollen but not painful.
Powdered; a way of preparing injectable medicine so that it does not have to be kept cold.
Health problems caused by not eating enough of the foods that the body needs.
(dry malnutrition) A condition caused by not eating enough. Starvation. The person is very thin and underweight, often with a pot belly.
Dark, olive-colored areas on face, breasts, or middle of the belly that are normal in a pregnant woman.
(breast abscess) An infection of the breast, usually in the first weeks or months of nursing a baby. It causes part of the breast to become hot, red, and swollen.
A thin, soft sheet or layer that lines or protects some part of an animal or plant.
(climacteric) The time when a woman naturally stops having monthly bleeding, usually between the ages of 40 and 50. Menstrual period, menstruation Monthly bleeding in women.
Of or relating to the mind (thinking, brain).
A tiny plant or animal so small it can only be seen with the aid of microscope.
An instrument with lenses that make very tiny objects look larger.
Something so small that it can only be seen with a microscope.
A severe, throbbing headache, sometimes on one side of the head only. It often causes vomiting. 425
(mg.) One thousandth of a gram.
(ml.) One thousandth of a liter.
Simple metals or other things the body needs, such as iron, calcium, and iodine.
(spontaneous abortion) The death of the developing baby or fetus in the womb, sometimes followed by heavy bleeding with blood clots.
(Down's syndrome) A disease in which a child is born mentally slow with slanted eyes, a round dull face, and wide hands with short fingers.
Nausea and vomiting that occur especially in the morning in the early months of pregnancy.
Artificial respiration. A method of helping a person who has stopped breathing to start breathing again.

A thick, slippery liquid that moistens and protects the linings of the nose, throat, stomach, guts, and vagina. Narrow-spectrum antibiotic A medicine that works against a limited number of different kinds of bacteria.
Of or relating to the nose.
Stomach distress or upset; feeling like you need to vomit.
Belly button; umbilicus; the place in the middle of the belly where the umbilical cord was attached.
Thin threads or strings that run from the brain to every part of the body and carry messages for feeling and movement.
A disease that does not spread from person to person.
Usual, natural, or average. Something that is normal has nothing wrong with it.
Nourishing. Nutritious foods are those that have the things the body needs to grow, be healthy, and fight off disease.
A condition of being blocked or clogged. An obstructed gut is a medical emergency.
A salve or lotion to use on the skin. *Ophthalmic Of the eye.
By mouth. An oral medicine is one taken by mouth.
A part of the body that is more or less complete in itself and does a specific job. For example, the lungs are organs for breathing.
Living things (animals or plants).
Having to do with the ears.
A measure of weight equal to about 28 grams. There are 16 ounces in one pound.
Small sacs in a woman's belly next to her womb. They produce the eggs that join with a man's sperm to make a baby.
Dangerous medicines that cause the womb and blood vessels in it to contract. They should only be used to control a mother's heavy bleeding after her child is born.
The roof or top part of the mouth.
An organ below the stomach, on the left side, that produces insulin.
Tiny blood vessels that appear in the top edge of the cornea in certain eye diseases, like trachoma.
Loss of the ability to move part or all of the body.
Worms and tiny animals that live in or on another animal or person and cause harm. Fleas, intestinal worms, and amebas are parasites.
Not by mouth but by injection.
The process of heating milk or other liquids to a certain temperature (60° C) for about 30 minutes in order to kill harmful bacteria. Pelvis Hip bones.
The thin lining between the guts and body wall. The bag that holds the guts.
A very dangerous inflammation of the peritoneum. The belly gets hard like a board, and the person is in great pain, especially when he tries to lie with his legs straight.
A rare kind of anemia caused by a lack of vitamin B12. Pernicious means harmful.
(petrolatum, Vaseline) A grease‐like jelly used in preparing skin ointments.
A store that sells medicines and health care supplies. 426
Mucus with pus that forms in abnormal amounts in the lungs and must be coughed out. Piles See Hemorrhoids. Pimples See Acne.
(afterbirth) The dark and spongy lining inside the womb where the fetus joins the mother's body. The placenta normally comes out 15 minutes to half an hour after the baby is born.

A condition in which the placenta is too low in the womb and blocks the mouth of the womb. The risk of dangerous bleeding is high. Women who have bleeding late in pregnancy—a possible sign of placenta previa—should go to a hospital at once.
A kind of banana with a lot of starch and fiber. It is often cooked and eaten when green.

The fine dust made in the flower of a seed plant. People who are allergic to pollen often have hay fever at times of the year when plants put a lot of this dust into the air. Postpartum After childbirth.

Heavy bleeding of the mother following childbirth. Power of suggestion or power of belief The influence of belief or strong ideas. For example, sick people can feel better because they have faith in a remedy, even if the remedy does not have any medical effect.
Care taken in advance to prevent harm or prepare for emergencies before they happen.
A dangerous condition during pregnancy, which can lead to seizures.
The period (normally 9 months) when a woman carries a child inside her.
A baby born before the full 9 months of pregnancy and weighing less than 2 kilos.
An abnormal position of delivery in which the baby's hand comes out first during the birth. This is an emergency needing a doctor.
Action taken to stop sickness before it starts.
The slipping or falling down of a part of the body from its normal position; for example, a prolapsed rectum or womb.
The word prophylactic means preventive, but condoms are sometimes called prophylactics.
A firm, muscular gland at the base of the man's urinary tube, or urethra. Often in older men the prostate becomes enlarged, causing difficulty in urinating.
Foods that are rich in vitamins and minerals. They help build healthy bodies and make people more able to resist or fight diseases.
Body-building foods necessary for proper growth and strength.
A fleshy growth that slowly extends from the edge of the eye onto the cornea.
The number of times a person's heart beats in one minute.
The round opening or black center in the iris of the eye. It gets smaller in bright light and larger in the dark.
A very strong laxative that causes diarrhea.
The number of times something happens in a given amount of time.
A very sharp pain in the abdomen that occurs after the belly is pressed firmly and slowly, when the hand is removed suddenly. This pain is a sign of an acute abdomen.
The end of the large intestine close to the anus.
An automatic reaction or movement that happens without a person's trying to do it.
Drink A drink to correct dehydration, which you can make with boiled water, salt, and sugar or powdered cereal.
The ability of something to defend itself against something that would normally harm or kill it. Many bacteria become resistant to the effects of certain antibiotics.
What is needed or available for doing or making something. People, land, animals, money, skills, and plants are resources that can be used for improving health.
Breathing. The respiratory system includes the bronchi, lungs, and other organs used in breathing.
The number of times a person breathes in one minute.
Abnormal slowness of though, action, or mental and emotional growth.
An inflammation of the lining of the nose, often caused by allergies. Hay fever. 427
The possibility of injury, loss, or harm. Danger.
To grow different crops one after the other in the same field, so that the soil becomes richer rather than weaker from year to year. Rupture See Hernia.
Public cleanliness involving community efforts in disease prevention, promoting hygiene, and keeping public places free of waste.
The bag between a man's legs that holds his testicles or balls.
Medicine that causes drowsiness or sleep.
A sudden, violent attack of a disease, causing convulsions or spasms (jerking of the body that the person cannot control) and sometimes unconsciousness.
An infection of the blood sometimes called 'blood poisoning'. Sexually transmitted infection (STI) A disease spread by sexual contact.
A dangerous condition with severe weakness or unconsciousness, cold sweat, and fast, weak pulse. It is caused by dehydration, hemorrhage, injury, burns, or a severe illness.
Problems caused by using a medicine.
The things or conditions one looks for when examining a sick person, to find out what sickness he has. In this book symptoms, or the problems a person feels, are included with signs.
(sinusitis) Sinuses are hollows in the bone that open into the nose. Sinusitis is inflammation causing pain above and below the eyes.
Fizzy, carbonated drinks like Coca-Cola. Soft spot See Fontanel.
A sudden muscle contraction that a person cannot control. Spasms of the gut produce cramps, or colic. Spasms of the bronchi occur in asthma. Spasms of the jaw and other muscles occur in tetanus.
Having chronic abnormal muscle contraction due to brain damage. The legs of spastic children often cross like scissors.
An organ normally the size of a fist under the lower edge of the ribs on the left side. Its job is to help make and filter the blood. Spontaneous abortion See Miscarriage.
(strain) Bruising, stretching, or tearing of ligaments or tendons in a twisted joint. A sprain is worse than a strain.
Mucus and pus (phlegm) coughed up from the lungs and bronchi of a sick person.
Energy foods like maize, rice, wheat, cassava, potatoes, and squash.
(1) Completely clean and free from living micro-organisms. Things are usually sterilized by boiling or heating. (2) Sterile also means permanently unable to have children.
(1) To sterilize instruments, bottles, and other things by boiling or heating in an oven. (2) Also a permanent way of making a man or a woman unable to reproduce (have children).
An instrument used to listen to sounds in the body, such as the heartbeat.
The sac-like organ in the belly where food is digested. In common language 'stomach' is often used to mean the whole belly or abdomen.
Shit. Bowel movement. See Feces.
(apoplexy, cerebro-vascular accident) A sudden loss of consciousness, feeling, or ability to move, caused by bleeding or a clot inside the brain. Also see heat stroke (p. 81).

However, it is more exact to determine dosage according to a person's weight. Information for doing this is sometimes included briefly in parentheses ( ), for use of health workers who have scales. If you read. . . (100mg./kg./day), this means 100 mg. per kilogram of body weight per day. In other words, during a 24 hour period you give 100 mg. of the medicine for each kilogram the person weighs. For example, suppose you want to give aspirin to a boy with rheumatic fever who weighs 36 kilograms. The recommended dose of aspirin for rheumatic fever is 100 mg./kg./day. So multiply: 100 mg. x 36 = 3600 mg. The boy should get 3600 mg. of aspirin a day. One aspirin tablet contains 300 mg. of aspirin, 3600 mg. comes to 12 tablets. So give the boy 2 tablets 6 times a day (or 2 tablets every 4 hours). This is one way to figure the dosages for different medicines. Antivenoms for scorpion sting should be used only in those areas where there are dangerous or deadly kinds of scorpions. Antivenoms are usually needed only when a small child is stung, especially if stung on the main upper part of the body or head. To do most good, the antivenom should be injected as soon as possible after the child has been stung. Antivenoms usually come with full instructions. Follow them carefully. Antivenoms, or medicines that protect the body against poisons, have been developed for the bites of poisonous snakes in many parts of the world. If you live where people are sometimes bitten or killed by poisonous snakes, find out what antivenoms are available, get them ahead of time, and keep them on hand. Some antivenoms—those in dried or 'lyophilized' form—can be kept without refrigeration. Others need to be kept cold. It is also used to control heavy bleeding after miscarriage or abortion. Oxytocin can be used to prevent or control severe bleeding of the mother after the baby is born and before or after the afterbirth comes out. (It also helps bring the afterbirth out, but should not be used for this unless there is severe bleeding or great delay.) It can also be used to control heavy bleeding after miscarriage or abortion. Dosage: To treat heavy bleeding, give 1 ml. (10 units) by intramuscular injection. If severe bleeding continues, inject another 1 ml. in 15 minutes. To prevent heavy bleeding after birth, give 1 ml. after the baby is born. Misoprostol (Cytotec)

Misoprostol can be used to prevent or control heavy bleeding after childbirth, and control heavy bleeding from miscarriage or abortion. It can also be used to end a pregnancy, but it is safer when taken with another medicine, mifepristone (see Where Women Have No Doctor for more information). Dosage for heavy bleeding: Give 600 mcg by mouth (dissolve tablets against the cheek or under the tongue and then swallow any remaining parts). If the woman is feeling nauseous, you can also put the tablets up her anus to dissolve there. FOR PILES (HEMORRHOIDS) Suppositories for hemorrhoids

These are special bullet-shaped tablets to be put up the anus. They help make hemorrhoids smaller and less painful. There are many different preparations. Those that are often most helpful, but are more expensive, contain cortisone or a cortico-steroid. Special ointments are also available. Diets to soften stools are important (see p. 126). Dosage: Put a suppository up the anus after the daily bowel movement, and another on going to bed. Powdered milk (dried milk)

For babies, mother's milk is best. It is rich in body-building vitamins and minerals. When breast milk is not available, other milk products—including powdered milk—can be used. To allow a baby to make full use of its food value, mix the powdered milk with some sugar and cooking oil (see p. 120). In 1 cup of boiled water, put: 12 level teaspoons of powdered milk, 2 level teaspoons of sugar, and 3 teaspoons of oil Mixed (or multi) vitamins These come in many forms, but tablets are usually cheapest and work well. Injections of vitamins are rarely necessary, are a waste of money, cause unnecessary pain and sometimes abscesses. Tonics and elixirs often do not have the most important vitamins and are usually too expensive for the good they do. Nutritious food is the best source of vitamins. If additional vitamins are needed, use vitamin tablets. In some cases of poor nutrition added vitamins may help, and multivitamins can be helpful for people with HIV. Be sure the tablets used contain all the important vitamins (see p. 118). Using standard tablets of mixed vitamins, 1 tablet daily is usually enough. For prevention: In areas where night blindness and xerophthalmia are common problems in children, they should eat more yellow fruits and vegetables and dark green leafy foods as well as animal foods, such as eggs and liver. Fish liver oil is high in vitamin A. Or vitamin A capsules can be given. Give 1 capsule once every 4 to 6 months— no more for prevention. Mothers can help prevent these eye problems in their babies by taking 1 vitamin A capsule (200,000 units) by mouth when their baby is born or within 1 month after giving birth. Children with measles are at especially high risk of xerophthalmia, and should be given vitamin A when the illness begins. In areas where children do not get enough vitamin A, added foods or capsules with vitamin A often help children survive measles and other serious illnesses. For treatment: Give 1 vitamin A capsule (200,000 units) by mouth, or an injection of 100,000 units. The next day give 1 vitamin A capsule (200,000 units) by mouth, and another capsule 1 to 2 weeks later. For children less than 1 year old, reduce all doses by one-half. medicines.x: (also in drops, mixtures, and elixirs for children) Ferrous sulfate is useful in the treatment or prevention of most anemias. Treatment with ferrous sulfate by mouth usually takes at least 3 months. If improvement does not take place, the anemia is probably caused by something other than lack of iron. Get medical help. If this is difficult, try treating with folic acid. Ferrous sulfate is especially important for pregnant women who may be anemic or malnourished. Iron may work best if it is taken with some vitamin C (either fruits and vegetables, or a vitamin C tablet). Ferrous sulfate sometimes upsets the stomach and is best taken with meals. Also, it can cause constipation, and it may make the stools (shit) look black. For children under 3 years, a piece of a tablet can be ground up very fine and mixed with the food. ferrous sulfate is poisonous. Keep tablets out of the reach of children. Do not give ferrous sulfate to severely malnourished persons. Dosage of ferrous sulfate for anemia: —using tablets of 200 mg.— Give 3 times a day, with meals. In each dose give: 1⁄4 tablet) ground up fine and mixed with food. Folic acid—for some kinds of anemia

Folic acid can be important in the treatment of kinds of anemia in which blood cells have been destroyed in the veins, as is the case with malaria. An anemic person who has a large spleen or looks yellow may need folic acid, especially if his anemia does not get much better with ferrous sulfate. Babies who are fed goat's milk and pregnant women who are anemic or malnourished often need folic acid as well as iron. Folic acid can be obtained by eating dark green leafy foods, meat, and liver, or by taking folic acid tablets. Usually 2 weeks treatment is enough for children, although in some areas children with sickle cell disease, or a kind of anemia called thalassemia may need it for years. Pregnant women who are anemic and malnourished would be helped by taking folic acid and iron tablets daily throughout pregnancy. Dosage of folic acid for anemia—using 5 mg. tablets: Give by mouth once a day. adults and children over 3 years: 1 tablet (5 mg.) (2 1⁄2 mg.) Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin)—for pernicious anemia only This is mentioned only to discourage its use. Vitamin B12 is useful only for a rare type of anemia that is almost never found except in some persons over 35 years whose ancestors are from northern Europe. Many doctors prescribe it when it is not needed, just to be giving their patients something. Do not waste your money on vitamin B12 or let a doctor or health worker give it to you unless a blood analysis has been done, and it has been shown that you have pernicious anemia. medicines.x: fee for putting it in: ______ An IUD must be inserted and removed by a trained health worker. The most common side effect is heavier, longer and more painful monthly bleeding, but this usually stops after the first 3 months. Occasionally an IUD will slip out of place. If this happens, it will not be effective in preventing pregnancy, so it is important for a woman with an IUD to learn to check it to make sure it is still in place. Most IUDs have 2 thread-like strings attached which hang down into the vagina. The woman should check the strings after each monthly bleeding to make sure the IUD is in place. To check the strings, she should wash her hands well and then reach as far as she can into the vagina with two fingers and feel for the IUD strings. Do not pull on the strings. If she cannot feel the strings, or if she can feel the hard part of the IUD, she needs to use a condom or another method of family planning until she can have the IUD checked by a trained health worker. For information on IUDs, see page 290. Pelvic inflammatory disease is the most serious problem that can result from having an IUD. Most infections happen in the first 3 months, usually because the woman already had an infection when the IUD was put in. Or it may happen because the health worker did not put in the IUD under clean conditions. If a woman with an IUD has any signs of infection she should see a trained health worker right away. danger.t: Losing a large amount of blood from anywhere in the body
do: Press hard on the wound with a clean cloth and keep pressing.
Raise the part above the level of the heart if you can.
Do not let go to look — keep the pressure on while someone brings help.

danger.t: Coughing up blood
do: Keep the person sitting up and calm.
Get to a health centre — this needs testing for TB.

danger.t: Lips or nails turning blue, if this is new
do: Sit the person upright and loosen tight clothing.
Get help now — this means the body is not getting enough air.

danger.t: Great difficulty breathing that does not improve with rest
do: Sit the person upright, leaning slightly forward.
Loosen anything tight around the chest and neck.
Get to help without delay.

danger.t: The person cannot be woken
do: Lay the person on their side so vomit can drain out.
Check that nothing is blocking the throat.
Do not give anything by mouth. Get help now.

danger.t: So weak that he faints when he stands up
do: Lay the person down with the legs raised.
Give sips of liquid once fully awake.
Get help.

danger.t: A day or more without being able to pass urine
do: Give liquids if the person can drink.
Get to a health worker — the bladder or kidneys may be blocked.

danger.t: A day or more without being able to drink any liquids
do: Try small sips of Rehydration Drink, a spoonful at a time.
If nothing stays down, get help now — fluid may be needed by another route.

danger.t: Heavy vomiting, or severe diarrhoea for more than a day — or more than a few hours in a baby
do: Start Rehydration Drink immediately and keep offering it.
Keep breastfeeding a baby.
Get help if the drink will not stay down.

danger.t: Black stools like tar, or vomit with blood in it
do: Give nothing but small sips of water.
Get to a health centre now — there is bleeding inside the gut.

danger.t: Strong continuous belly pain with vomiting, in someone with no diarrhoea who cannot pass stool
do: Give nothing by mouth — no food, no water, no laxative, no enema.
Do not give pain medicine; it hides the signs.
Go to a hospital at once. This may need an operation.

danger.t: Any strong continuous pain lasting more than 3 days
do: Note where the pain is and what makes it worse.
Have it examined by a health worker.

danger.t: Stiff neck with arched back, with or without a stiff jaw
do: Keep the person quiet in a dark, cool place.
Do not delay — this can be meningitis or tetanus.
Go now, and say what you have seen when you arrive.

danger.t: More than one fit in someone with fever or serious illness
do: Clear the space around the person; do not hold them down.
Put nothing in the mouth.
Once it stops, lay them on their side and go for help.

danger.t: High fever above 39°C that cannot be brought down, or lasts more than 4 or 5 days
do: Cool the body with wet cloths and fan the skin.
Give acetaminophen and plenty of liquids.
If the fever will not come down, go for help.

danger.t: Weight loss over an extended time
do: Have this examined — TB and other long illnesses begin this way.

danger.t: Blood in the urine
do: Give plenty of liquids.
Have it examined — do not treat this at home.

danger.t: Sores that keep growing and do not go away with treatment
do: Keep the sore clean and covered.
Have it looked at by a health worker.

danger.t: A lump anywhere in the body that keeps getting bigger
do: Do not squeeze or cut it.
Have it examined.

danger.t: In pregnancy: any bleeding, a swollen face with trouble seeing late on, a long delay after the waters break, or heavy bleeding
do: Lie down on the left side.
Send for a midwife or get to a health centre at once.
Keep a note of how much bleeding there has been.
